source.title: On the Privacy Effect of Data Enhancement via the Lens of Memorization
source.authors: Xiao Li; Qiong-Xiu Li; Zhan Hu; Xiao-Lin Hu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how membership-inference attack performance relates to the train-test accuracy gap across data-enhancement methods, using different measures of privacy leakage. It does not test the claim versions’ specified interventions or outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports train/test accuracy and attack results for augmentation and adversarial-training settings. Its direct result bearing on the claim is the reported correlation between attack performance and train-test gap; broader training-accuracy tables are not extracted as separate claim rows. Values used only to choose augmentation hyperparameters are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study measures membership-inference performance and its association with the train-test accuracy gap. None of its own results tests V1–V8. Using memorization scores from Feldman and Zhang does not test V8's removal-and-retraining result.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly paraphrases the correlation conclusion. The authors also conclude that label smoothing does not consistently increase privacy leakage, adversarial training increases memorization and privacy leakage relative to standard training, and greater adversarial robustness among adversarially trained models need not increase privacy leakage.
record.recipe_differences: Studies privacy leakage using membership inference and memorization scores, rather than the claim versions’ interventions and generalization outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Correlation varies with attack measure (LiRA versus MaxPreCA) and dataset; the paper reports different correlations across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Purchases, and Locations.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the recorded augmentation settings, LiRA performance correlates less strongly with the train-test accuracy gap than MaxPreCA performance: 0.221 versus 0.708 on CIFAR-10, 0.307 versus 0.454 on CIFAR-100, 0.504 versus 0.803 on SVHN, 0.015 versus 0.292 on Purchases, and 0.457 versus 0.835 on Locations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The measured association between membership-inference vulnerability and the train-test accuracy gap depends on the attack and dataset; memorization-consistent attacks can show weaker associations.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
record.problems: Correlation findings are reported for attack metrics across data-enhancement models and do not establish causation. The text notes that TPR @ 0.001% FPR results were unstable, so the main analysis uses TPR @ 0.1% FPR. Some correlation values are presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Tables II, III, B.1, D.1, or D.2: their enhancement-specific privacy and accuracy numbers do not measure the correlation between privacy leakage and train-test gap as extracted here. Figure 3 reports plotted correlations for CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN; Figure 8 reports Purchases and Locations. Other figures and tables concern privacy attack performance, augmentation, or adversarial robustness rather than a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No fixed-random-label fitting experiment or random-label held-out accuracy comparison. Disturblabel's training-time label corruption does not supply this comparison.
No width sweep beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image task.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No batch-size comparison or evaluation of remedies for large-batch penalties.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures. AWP results alone do not test that correlation.
No removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples followed by retraining and test-accuracy measurement.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. The paper cites the benefits of memorizing long-tailed examples as prior work rather than independently testing V8. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on random labels or compare held-out accuracy against chance; its natural-label accuracy results do not test the stated coexistence.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Does not test dropout or joint dropout and weight-decay removal.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- or margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain to measure test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Measured LiRA attack success rate against train-test accuracy gap across data-augmentation models.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between TPR @ 0.1% FPR and train-test gap
rows.note: The text reports the correlation and says it is much lower than for MaxPreCA; this measures privacy-attack performance versus the gap, not whether the generalization-gap claim versions hold.
rows.check: The reported r=0.221 measures privacy-attack performance versus generalization gap, which no listed version claims.
